summary: The note examines the environmental burden of construction and demolition (C&D) waste in the US and the strategies emerging to recycle it. It covers economic incentives, circular economy design, AI sorting and concrete crushing, workforce training, and challenges such as mixed waste, limited infrastructure and competition from virgin materials. It concludes that collaboration among government, industry and communities is needed.
one_line: Overview of strategies, technologies, training efforts and obstacles in recycling construction and demolition waste in the United States.
key_facts: The EPA reports that over 600 million tons of C&D debris were generated in the United States in 2023.
C&D waste includes concrete, wood, metals, asphalt, and gypsum, the latter often found in drywall.
As of October 10, 2023, a substantial proportion of C&D waste is still disposed of in landfills, though recycling rates are rising.
In December 2023 the Department of Environmental Conservation unveiled two strategies for C&D waste recycling: economic incentives for materials recovery and circular economy technologies.
Charlotte, North Carolina introduced a rebate program for construction companies that demonstrate high waste diversion and recycling, launched in September 2023.
Tom Richardson, Charlotte's waste management coordinator, said the city is seeing a promising increase in recycling since the initiative launched.
Architect Sarah Jennings of Innovative Design Solutions praised circular economy principles, including designing buildings with deconstruction in mind to enable material reuse.
GreenSort Tech's AI-powered sorting robots have been implemented in Dallas, Texas, since November 2023 to separate waste types accurately.
Recent concrete crushing technologies allow demolished concrete to be reused as aggregate in new construction projects.
Mike Anderson, founder of the Construction Recycling Alliance, said on December 15, 2023 that a skilled workforce is crucial to improving recycling rates.
Local governments and organizations have rolled out educational campaigns and workshops on best practices in C&D recycling.
Key challenges include difficulty separating mixed waste on demolition sites, which can contaminate recyclables and reduce their quality.
Many regions lack recycling infrastructure, and building new facilities requires substantial public and private investment.
Recycled construction materials must compete with virgin materials, which are often more cost-effective due to existing supply chains.
